translations.answer: Average frequency equality does not imply strict synchronization of instantaneous production and consumption. Python scheduling, ROS transmission, and batch write-inflated data cause bursts; if the queue is full and new targets are discarded, the execution layer continues to consume old trajectories, leading to increasing delays and target jumps upon recovery. Double-ended monotonic clocks and queue watermarks should be recorded, and bounded buffers, expired command discarding, and target continuity protection should be set.
translations.applicability: Applicable to command bridging between non-real-time upper and high-frequency servo layers; specific conclusions must be verified with local timestamps.
translations.credibility.rationale: The solution has not closed or there is a conflict in the source; the conclusion is not yet verified or reproducible.
translations.details.attempts.0: Divide each 20 ms command into 5 parts for 4 ms execution by the execution layer.
translations.details.attempts.1: Discard 1/5 of the messages to reduce queue growth.
translations.details.attempts.2: Plan to switch the Python middle layer to C++.
translations.details.diagnostics.0: Record the upper-level production timestamp, lower-level consumption timestamp, queue depth, packet loss count, and target continuity.
translations.details.environments.0: Upper-level remote operation at 50 Hz/20 ms; lower-level C++ execution at 250 Hz/4 ms; ROS topic; maximum queue of 5000, cumulative 10 messages after execution.
translations.details.limits.0: Raises questions about the factual basis of the total bus; no public timestamp curve, packet loss rate, or final rewrite result is provided.
translations.details.outcomes.0: First solution still causes queue overflow; second solution reduces delay but causes underload jitter; final C++ rewrite direction is not publicly verified.
translations.details.problem_statements.0: How to stably send 50 Hz upper-level commands to the 250 Hz lower-level execution loop?
translations.details.problem_statements.1: Why does queue overflow and queue underflow both manifest as robot jitter?
translations.details.safety_notes.0: Limit joint speed, position increments, and torque during real machine testing; maintain the last safe target or enter damping mode when queue is abnormal; do not directly convert missing frames into abrupt jumps.
translations.details.suspected_causes.0: Inconsistent time/scheduling between Python and C++ endpoints.
translations.details.suspected_causes.1: Fixed five-part interpolation does not handle network jitter and production-consumption offset.
translations.details.symptoms.0: Queue overflow discards new messages, leading to long delays and sudden large oscillations.
translations.details.symptoms.1: Delay decreases after discarding 1/5 of the messages, but the queue is exhausted and continues to jitter.
translations.media_summaries.0: The Mermaid diagram in the text explains the structure of upper-level asynchronous write to queue and lower-level strict periodic read from queue; the diagram is conceptual and not real-time sequence evidence.
translations.source.locator: Description of the phenomenon, queue overflow message, and visible comments that question the facts.
translations.source.title: Why does queue overflow and underflow cause burst oscillations when bridging 50 Hz remote operation to 250 Hz execution layer?
